prod_010:n1.prompt:
You are helping me assemble the incident timeline for a resolved incident, as the first step in our postmortem process. We use {{vendor}} as our incident-management tool. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) the incident ID or name/date to identify the record, (2) my configured {{vendor}} credentials access, and (3) any specific channels (chat, alerting, paging) that were involved so you can cross-reference them.

Actions to take:
1. Retrieve the full incident record from {{vendor}}, including all status updates, timestamps, responder actions, and any linked chat or call transcripts/notes.
2. Reconstruct a clean chronological timeline: when the incident was detected, key alerts fired, actions taken by responders, decisions made, escalations, and resolution time.
3. Note any gaps, ambiguous timestamps, or missing context in the record, and flag these clearly rather than guessing.
4. Capture contributing factors and follow-up items mentioned in the incident chatter or updates, organized separately from the raw timeline, since these will feed the postmortem draft.
5. Format the output as a structured timeline document (chronological list with timestamps, actor, action/event) suitable for human review and for drafting the blameless write-up in the next step.

What done looks like: a complete, timestamped timeline covering incident start to resolution, with contributing factors and candidate follow-up actions noted separately, and any data gaps explicitly flagged.

Report back with: the assembled timeline document, a short summary of the incident (start time, detection method, resolution time, total duration), a list of flagged gaps/ambiguities needing human clarification, and confirmation that the record is ready to hand off for postmortem drafting. Do not attempt to publish, finalize, or share this timeline externally — this is preparation only for internal review.

prod_010:n2.prompt:
You are helping me draft a blameless postmortem for an incident that has already been resolved. Write it as a shared doc in {{vendor}}, our project-management workspace, using my configured credentials.

Ask me for anything below that you can't find:
- The incident identifier or title, and where its timeline lives. This could be an existing timeline doc or notes in {{vendor}}, or an export from our incident tooling.
- Incident start, detection, mitigation and resolution times, plus the affected services and customers.
- The workspace, project or space where postmortems belong in {{vendor}}.
- Who responded, listed by role, not by name.

Steps:
1. Gather the assembled timeline and related notes. If {{vendor}} has AI search across workspace content, use it to find relevant discussion, and keep its citations so every claim links back to its source.
2. Create a new doc in the right place in {{vendor}}, titled "Postmortem: [incident title] ([date])".
3. Draft it with these sections:
   - Summary
   - Impact: duration, users affected, severity
   - Timeline, with timestamps in UTC
   - Root cause and contributing factors
   - Detection and response: what worked and what didn't
   - Lessons learned
   - Proposed follow-up actions, each with a suggested owner role and priority
   - Open questions for the review meeting
4. Keep the language blameless:
   - Describe systems, processes and decisions, not individual fault.
   - Never write "X caused" about a person.
   - Mark anything uncertain as [TO CONFIRM] instead of guessing.
5. Do not file follow-up tasks or post anything publicly yet. Those are later steps.

You're done when a complete draft doc exists in {{vendor}} with every section filled in or explicitly marked [TO CONFIRM], and every timeline entry has a source.

Report back with:
- The doc link or location.
- A 3–5 sentence summary of the root cause.
- The list of [TO CONFIRM] items.
- The proposed follow-up actions, so I can bring them to the review.

prod_010:n3.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for a postmortem review meeting for a recently resolved incident. You cannot attend or run the live discussion yourself — holding the actual meeting remains a human step. Your job is to prepare everything needed so the meeting runs smoothly.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already available: the incident ID or name, links to the incident timeline/tooling (e.g., paging system, chat logs, monitoring dashboards), the draft blameless write-up if one exists, and the list of people who should attend (responders, service owners, any stakeholders).

Then do the following:
1. Pull together a concise pre-read: incident summary, timeline of key events, impact, and current draft root-cause hypotheses, using whatever draft write-up or timeline data I provide.
2. Draft a meeting agenda covering: timeline walkthrough, contributing factors discussion, blameless framing reminder, and follow-up action brainstorming.
3. Prepare a list of open questions or gaps in the timeline that the group should resolve during discussion.
4. Draft a proposed list of attendees and a suggested meeting length based on incident severity.
5. Prepare a template for capturing follow-up actions (owner, description, due date) to be filled in live during the meeting.

Once this package is ready, present it to me as a single organized document (pre-read, agenda, open questions, attendee list, action-item template) for me to review and send out ahead of the meeting.

Done looks like: a complete, ready-to-send meeting packet with no unresolved placeholders, plus a short summary of what's included and what decisions or scheduling I still need to handle myself. Since actually holding the discussion and scheduling attendance is a human step, stop for human sign-off once the packet is ready — do not attempt to run, simulate, or summarize a meeting that hasn't happened yet.

prod_010:n4.prompt:
You are helping me file the follow-up actions from a resolved incident's postmortem into {{vendor}}, our project tracker. Every corrective action should become a trackable item with a clear owner and due date so nothing agreed in the review gets lost.

Inputs to ask me for if missing:
- The incident identifier and title, plus a link to the postmortem write-up.
- The final list of corrective actions agreed in the review. For each one I need a short description, the owner (a teammate's name or email), a due date, and a priority if we set one.
- Where items should go in {{vendor}}: the team, project, or list, and any label or tag we use for incident follow-ups.

Steps:
1. Use your configured credentials to connect to {{vendor}} through its documented public API.
2. Check the target team or project for existing items that already cover an action. Do not create duplicates. Flag likely matches to me instead.
3. Match each owner to a {{vendor}} user. If an owner can't be matched unambiguously, ask me before assigning.
4. Create one task or issue per action, using the task-creation operation. Give each item a clear, action-oriented title. In the description, include the incident ID and a link to the postmortem. Set the assignee, due date, priority, and the incident follow-up label.
5. If {{vendor}} supports linking related items or a parent item, group all follow-ups under the incident so they can be tracked together.

Done looks like this: every agreed action exists exactly once in {{vendor}}, with an assignee, due date, label, and postmortem link.

Report back with a table showing each action, its created item's ID and link, owner, due date, and priority. Also list anything you skipped, any ambiguous owners you resolved with me, any duplicates you found, and any errors returned by {{vendor}}.

prod_010:n5.prompt:
You are helping me publish the public status-page write-up and customer comms for a recently resolved incident, using our {{vendor}} incident-management account (I'll provide login/API access via my configured credentials).

Before starting, ask me for anything missing:
- The incident ID/name in {{vendor}} and a link to its internal timeline or postmortem draft
- The customer-facing severity/impact summary (what broke, who was affected, when)
- Whether this is a new public incident post or an update to an existing one on our status page
- Any specific subscriber groups (customers vs internal stakeholders) that need notifying
- Our house style for public comms (tone, level of technical detail allowed)

Then do the following:
1. Pull the resolved incident's timeline and key facts from {{vendor}}.
2. Draft a blameless, customer-facing write-up: what happened, customer impact, resolution, and any follow-up commitments — using plain language, no internal jargon or blame.
3. Prepare the status-page entry in {{vendor}} (title, affected components, timeline of public-facing updates, final resolution note) as a draft, not yet published.
4. Prepare the subscriber notification content (for customers subscribed to the public status page, and separately for internal stakeholders who subscribe to structured updates without joining the war room), matching {{vendor}}'s notification channels.
5. Confirm the custom domain and branding settings on the public status page look correct if applicable.
6. Compile a short checklist showing: draft write-up text, draft notification text, target audiences, and any open questions or missing facts.

Publishing the status page and sending customer notifications is an external communication that affects customers and our public record, so after preparing everything, stop for human sign-off — do not publish the status page or send any notifications yourself.

Report back with: the drafted write-up, the drafted notifications, the checklist, and a clear note that this is ready for review and manual publish/send.
